subject: dsp
title: Fourier Analysis and Practical DSP
summary: Read calibrated spectra, follow changing frequencies, convert sample rates and verify an end-to-end measurement.

lessons.title: What a Fourier bin measures
lessons.summary: Turn a finite sample record into frequency components and label its bins correctly.
lessons.body:
A time plot shows when samples rise and fall. A **discrete Fourier transform**, or **DFT**, describes that same finite record as a combination of regularly spaced sinusoidal patterns. Each **frequency bin** tests one of those patterns across the whole record.

A strong match produces a large coefficient. Each coefficient is complex: its two parts preserve both magnitude and phase. The raw magnitude is not yet a calibrated tone amplitude. The **fast Fourier transform**, or **FFT**, is an efficient way to calculate these same DFT coefficients; it adds no observations.

## What a bin tells you

Imagine comparing the samples with a steady oscillation. At the matching rhythm, contributions reinforce each other. At many mismatched rhythms, positive and negative contributions cancel. The DFT does this with both cosine and sine components, so it can also describe where the oscillation is within its cycle.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: checking a rhythm
> Clap at a chosen steady rhythm while watching a repeating movement. A matching rhythm stays aligned; a mismatched rhythm drifts.
>
> **How it maps:** Each DFT bin tests one rhythm across the full record. Adding contributions reinforces a matching pattern and cancels many mismatched ones.
>
> **Where it stops:** A DFT uses signed and complex arithmetic to measure phase as well as strength; simply counting claps cannot reproduce it.

The transform describes the finite record exactly, within numerical error. It does not establish that a physical machine contains only the bin frequencies. A single tone between bins can produce several large coefficients. Do not count non-zero bins as separate physical oscillators.

## Label the frequency axis

The sample rate sets the physical time scale. The transform length sets how many frequency positions share that scale. With no padding, recording more samples at the same rate gives closer bin labels. Changing the sample rate without updating the labels gives the wrong frequency axis.

```formula essential
Δf = F_s / N
f_k = kΔf
where
Δf: spacing between neighbouring DFT bins, in hertz (Hz)
F_s: sample rate, in samples per second, expressed in Hz
N: number of acquired samples and transform points, with no zero padding
f_k: frequency of non-negative bin k, in Hz
k: non-negative integer bin index
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: bin spacing is the sample rate divided by the unpadded record length; each non-negative bin is another step along that grid.
```

Eight samples taken at 800 samples per second give non-negative labels of 0, 100, 200, 300 and 400 Hz. These labels exist even when a bin's coefficient is zero.

## Choose the transform for the input

For real input, the negative-frequency coefficients are complex conjugates of the positive-frequency coefficients: they carry redundant information. NumPy's `rfft` keeps the non-negative half. Interior coefficients can still be complex even though the samples are real.

An even-length real record includes DC and an exact Nyquist endpoint; an odd-length record has no bin exactly at Nyquist. For arbitrary complex input, negative frequencies can hold independent information, so use the full `fft`.

Use matching frequency-label functions. `rfftfreq` labels the real-input output; `fftfreq` labels the full output in stored order: zero, positive frequencies, then negative frequencies. For an even length, the full transform labels its Nyquist slot negative while the real-input transform labels it positive. Both describe the same sampled endpoint.

## Key takeaways

- A bin measures a pattern across a finite record; it is not proof of a separate physical tone.
- An FFT calculates a DFT efficiently, with no extra information.
- Match the frequency axis to the sample rate, transform length and real or complex input.

## Further reading

- [NumPy: DFT definitions and conventions](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.fft.html)
- [NumPy: real-input FFT](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)
- [NumPy: real-input frequency labels](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfftfreq.html)

questions.prompt: You acquire twice as many samples from a steady signal at the same sample rate, without padding. What happens to the non-negative FFT bin labels?

options.text: They become more closely spaced, while the Nyquist boundary stays the same
options.explanation: Correct. A longer acquired record puts more frequency positions inside the same sampling-frequency range.

options.text: Their spacing stays the same, but the Nyquist boundary doubles
options.explanation: The sample rate determines the Nyquist boundary; more samples at that rate make the unpadded grid finer.

options.text: Only bins containing physical tones receive labels
options.explanation: Every returned coefficient has a grid label, including coefficients with zero or very small magnitude.

questions.workedExample:
1. The sample rate has not changed, so the frequency scale and Nyquist boundary stay fixed.
2. The longer acquired record has more transform points.
3. Those points divide the same range into smaller steps. This changes the grid; a non-zero bin still need not represent a separate physical tone.

questions.prompt: A colleague says an FFT is a different transform that adds frequency information unavailable to a DFT. What is the best correction?

options.text: An FFT returns only amplitudes, while a DFT returns only phases
options.explanation: Both calculate complex transform coefficients that preserve magnitude and phase information.

options.text: An FFT is an efficient algorithm for calculating a DFT
options.explanation: Correct. Efficiency changes how the coefficients are computed, not what finite transform they represent.

options.text: An FFT removes all between-bin leakage
options.explanation: Leakage is a finite-record/window issue and remains when that DFT is evaluated by an FFT.

questions.workedExample:
1. The DFT defines the finite weighted sums, one per bin.
2. An FFT reorganises that calculation to reuse work.
3. Given the same convention and input, the coefficients agree within numerical error; no additional observation has been made.

questions.prompt: You are choosing between a full FFT and a real-input FFT. Which statements are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Negative frequencies can hold independent information for complex input
options.explanation: Correct. Real-input conjugate symmetry cannot be assumed for arbitrary complex records.

options.text: An odd-length real record always includes an exact Nyquist bin
options.explanation: The highest returned bin for an odd length is below the Nyquist frequency.

options.text: Real-input coefficients have redundant negative-frequency partners
options.explanation: Correct. Their conjugate symmetry permits a compact real-input transform.

options.text: A real-input FFT coefficient is always a real number
options.explanation: Interior coefficients are generally complex even when every input sample is real.

questions.workedExample:
1. Real samples impose conjugate symmetry on their full DFT.
2. The real-input transform retains enough coefficients to reconstruct that redundancy.
3. General complex input has no such guarantee, so retain both sides.
4. Whether a Nyquist coefficient exists depends on the parity of the record length, not merely on the input being real.

lessons.title: Calibrating a spectrum
lessons.summary: Recover real-tone amplitudes without doubling DC or Nyquist, and distinguish amplitude from power density.
lessons.body:
A raw FFT magnitude is a sum over samples. A longer record can therefore produce a larger raw peak even when the physical tone has stayed equally strong. Before interpreting a spectrum, ask what its vertical axis measures and how the software normalises it.

An **amplitude spectrum** reports tone size in the input's units, such as volts. A **power spectral density**, or **PSD**, reports mean-square content per unit bandwidth. They answer different questions and need different scaling.

## Turn a raw peak into a tone amplitude

Start with a controlled case: NumPy's default unnormalised forward FFT, a real record, no tapering window and an isolated tone exactly centred on an interior bin. A **bin-centred** tone completes a whole number of cycles in the record.

Divide the coefficient magnitude by the acquired sample count. Then double it for an ordinary positive-frequency tone: a real sinusoid has matching positive and negative frequency contributions, and a one-sided amplitude plot combines that pair.

```formula reference
A_k = (2|X[k]|) / N
where
A_k: peak amplitude of the isolated bin-centred real sinusoid, in the input signal's units
X[k]: unnormalised complex DFT coefficient at interior positive-frequency bin k
|X[k]|: non-negative magnitude of that complex coefficient
N: acquired sample count, with no padding or tapering window
k: positive-frequency bin with a distinct negative-frequency partner, excluding DC and Nyquist
In words: for an isolated bin-centred real tone without a taper, divide the raw bin magnitude by the acquired sample count and double it to combine the positive and negative frequency contributions.
```

If the same steady tone is recorded for twice as long, the raw magnitude doubles under these assumptions; the calibrated amplitude stays the same. That is a useful check for a length-dependent calibration bug.

## Treat the endpoints separately

DC has no separate negative-frequency partner. Neither does the Nyquist bin in an even-length real record. Divide their magnitudes by the sample count without doubling. For odd lengths, every returned real-FFT bin after DC has a partner because there is no exact Nyquist bin.

DC magnitude gives the absolute mean. To preserve the sign of an offset, use the signed real DC coefficient instead. The Nyquist component describes an alternating sampled sequence; it cannot establish an arbitrary continuous sinusoid's amplitude because sampling exactly at Nyquist has phase ambiguity.

Changing the FFT normalisation or applying a window changes the calibration. An off-bin tone spreads across bins, so its largest bin alone generally underestimates its peak even after this simple correction.

## Choose the quantity you need

Peak amplitude is useful for asking how large an isolated vibration or voltage tone is. Mean-square power describes a signal's average squared size. An ordinary sinusoid, averaged over whole cycles, contributes half its squared peak amplitude to mean square. Electrical watts require an additional circuit relationship; square volts alone are not watts.

PSD distributes mean-square power over frequency. For voltage input, its units are square volts per hertz. Multiplying each density by its bin width and summing estimates mean square under the estimator's window and detrending conventions. More densely spaced bins must not create extra total power.

SciPy's `periodogram` offers `scaling="density"` for PSD and `scaling="spectrum"` for a squared-magnitude spectrum. Its default detrending removes the mean; use `detrend=False` if DC must remain. Tapered PSD uses window-energy normalisation, so simply squaring doubled tone amplitudes is not a general PSD recipe. A tapered estimate also need not match the unweighted finite record's mean square exactly.

## Key takeaways

- Record the FFT normalisation, window, sample count and units before interpreting a peak.
- Combine paired bins for one-sided tone amplitude; leave DC and an even-length Nyquist bin undoubled.
- Choose amplitude for tone size and PSD for mean-square content per bandwidth.

## Further reading

- [NumPy: FFT normalisation conventions](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.fft.html)
- [SciPy: periodogram scaling and units](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.periodogram.html)

questions.prompt: You record the same isolated, bin-centred real cosine for twice as long at the same rate, using no taper. Its default NumPy FFT peak doubles. What should happen to the calibrated peak amplitude?

options.text: It should double because the raw FFT peak doubled
options.explanation: The raw transform sums over twice as many samples. Its increase alone does not show a stronger physical tone.

options.text: It should halve because the record is longer
options.explanation: The coefficient and sample-count denominator grow together, so the calibrated result does not halve.

options.text: It should stay the same after the sample-count and paired-bin corrections
options.explanation: Correct. The longer sum is offset by dividing by the longer record; the same real tone still has positive and negative partners.

questions.workedExample:
1. The physical input tone has the same peak in both records.
2. Under the stated coherent, untapered assumptions, doubling record length doubles its raw coefficient.
3. Calibration also divides by twice as many acquired samples.
4. Combining the paired real-tone bins therefore gives the same peak amplitude.

questions.prompt: You calibrate a default NumPy real FFT of an even-length, untapered record. Which operations are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Divide DC magnitude by record length without doubling
options.explanation: Correct. DC has no distinct negative-frequency partner.

options.text: Double the Nyquist magnitude after dividing by record length
options.explanation: The even-length Nyquist coefficient is unpaired and must not be doubled.

options.text: Double paired interior magnitudes after dividing by record length
options.explanation: Correct under the isolated, bin-centred real-tone assumptions.

options.text: Use DC magnitude to recover the sign of the mean
options.explanation: Magnitude discards the sign; the signed real DC coefficient is needed for that.

questions.workedExample:
1. Pair positive and negative frequencies for ordinary real sinusoids.
2. DC and the even-length Nyquist slot each represent a single unpaired component.
3. Therefore double interior magnitudes only.
4. Taking a magnitude also discards the sign of the mean, so retain the real DC coefficient when that sign is needed.

questions.prompt: A vibration analyser reports a PSD for voltage input. Which interpretation is appropriate?

options.text: It is peak voltage at each frequency
options.explanation: PSD is mean-square content per bandwidth, not a peak-amplitude spectrum.

options.text: Its units are square volts per hertz; integrate over bandwidth to estimate mean square
options.explanation: Correct. Multiplying each density by its bin width and summing estimates the corresponding mean-square contribution.

options.text: It measures electrical watts without knowing the circuit
options.explanation: Mean-square voltage needs a circuit relationship, such as a known resistance, to become electrical power in watts.

questions.workedExample:
1. Voltage amplitude has units of volts.
2. Squared voltage has units of square volts.
3. A density divides that mean-square quantity by bandwidth, giving square volts per hertz.
4. Summing density times frequency-bin width estimates mean square, under the estimator's window and detrending conventions.

lessons.title: Finite records and spectral leakage
lessons.summary: Choose a named window, understand its trade-offs and correct coherent tone amplitude.
lessons.body:
A noiseless single tone can produce many non-zero FFT bins. The transform describes a finite record as a repeating pattern. If the tone does not complete a whole number of cycles, joining repeated copies can create an abrupt boundary. Several bin patterns are needed to represent that record: **spectral leakage**.

This does not mean the FFT created sensor noise or discovered a separate oscillator at every bin. It means the finite observation affects the spectrum you can measure.

## A window changes the leakage pattern

An unweighted record uses a **rectangular window**. A **spectral window** multiplies the samples by a chosen set of weights before transforming. A taper gives less weight to the ends, reducing the effect of the repeated boundary.

The central feature around a tone is its **main lobe**; smaller surrounding features are **side lobes**. Compared with a rectangular window, a Hann window lowers side lobes but widens the main lobe. A weak tone far from a strong one can become easier to see, while two close tones can become harder to separate. Choose according to the distinction the measurement needs.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a photograph's soft edge
> A hard-edged cut-out draws attention to its boundary. Fading the edge makes that boundary less abrupt, but blurs where it ends.
>
> **How it maps:** A taper reduces abrupt record boundaries and distant spectral leakage, while broadening a tone's central spectral feature.
>
> **Where it stops:** The broadening comes from Fourier mathematics, not optical focus. A window cannot reveal unrecorded samples or guarantee separation of nearby tones.

## Name the finite window you used

SciPy distinguishes a **periodic Hann window**, requested with `sym=False`, from a symmetric Hann, requested with `sym=True`. The periodic version is intended for spectral analysis; the symmetric version is commonly used for FIR design. A periodic window's final stored value need not be zero.

Their finite arrays have different sums. The average weight, called **coherent gain**, describes how the window scales a coherent tone under the usual separated-tone assumptions. For a periodic Hann with more than two samples, that average is one half. A symmetric Hann's average differs, so calculate the actual weight sum instead of assuming both conventions are interchangeable.

## Calibrate the tone you actually measured

For an isolated, bin-centred real tone at an interior frequency, replace the unwindowed sample-count denominator with the sum of the weights. This is exact when the mirrored negative-frequency tone contributes zero at the measured positive bin, and approximate when that contribution is negligible. Check the condition near DC or Nyquist and when changing windows.

```formula reference
A_k = (2|X_w[k]|) / S
S = Σ w[n]
where
A_k: estimated peak amplitude of the isolated bin-centred real tone, in the input signal's units
X_w[k]: unnormalised DFT coefficient of the windowed samples at interior positive-frequency bin k
|X_w[k]|: magnitude of the complex coefficient
k: bin where the mirrored negative-frequency tone contributes zero or negligibly
S: sum of all unitless window weights
Σ: add the weights for all acquired samples
w[n]: unitless window weight at sample index n
n: integer sample index across the acquired record
In words: for an isolated bin-centred tone whose positive and negative responses do not interfere, divide twice the windowed bin magnitude by the actual sum of window weights to estimate its peak amplitude.
```

This corrects window attenuation; it does not fix every peak error. A tone between bins can still have an underestimated largest bin, called **scalloping loss**. Nearby signals can also affect the peak. Noise PSD needs a different calibration based on squared weights and sample rate; use a documented estimator rather than reusing the coherent-tone correction.

## Key takeaways

- Leakage comes from finite observation and does not require noise.
- Hann suppresses side lobes while broadening the central response.
- State the window convention and distinguish coherent-tone correction from off-bin estimation and PSD scaling.

## Further reading

- [SciPy: Hann conventions](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.windows.hann.html)
- [Steven W. Smith: applications of the DFT](https://www.dspguide.com/CH9.PDF)
- [SciPy: window sums and spectral scaling](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/tutorial/signal.html#spectral-analysis)

questions.prompt: A noiseless sinusoid does not complete a whole number of cycles in a rectangular record. Its FFT shows many non-zero bins. What is the most relevant explanation?

options.text: Spectral leakage from the finite record
options.explanation: Correct. A tone between DFT bins spreads across the finite-record spectrum even without noise.

options.text: The FFT has created random sensor noise
options.explanation: The transform is deterministic; the spread does not require random noise.

options.text: Every non-zero bin proves a separate physical oscillator
options.explanation: Many non-zero coefficients can describe one off-bin tone through the record's window response.

questions.workedExample:
1. The DFT represents the finite record as a repeating pattern.
2. A fractional number of tone cycles generally creates an abrupt repeated boundary.
3. Multiple DFT components are needed to describe that record, so many bins can be non-zero without multiple physical tones.

link.title: Smith: spectral analysis of finite signals

questions.prompt: A coherent tone appears smaller after applying a Hann window. You want its peak amplitude, under the separated positive/negative response assumptions. Which calibration choice is sound?

options.text: Use the original sample count and ignore the window
options.explanation: This leaves the taper attenuation in the result, underestimating the coherent tone.

options.text: Double every returned bin, including DC and Nyquist
options.explanation: DC and an even-length Nyquist endpoint are unpaired. Window correction does not change that rule.

options.text: Use the actual sum of window weights and combine only the paired tone bins
options.explanation: Correct. The weight sum corrects coherent attenuation, and paired-bin scaling accounts for the real sinusoid.

questions.workedExample:
1. Tapering changes the raw coefficient even when the physical tone has not changed.
2. Correct coherent attenuation using the sum of the weights actually applied.
3. Combine the positive and negative contributions for this interior real tone.
4. Keep the assumptions explicit: this does not guarantee an exact largest-bin amplitude for an off-bin tone or replace PSD normalisation.

questions.prompt: Which statements should accompany a Hann-window spectrum? Select all that apply.

options.text: Specify whether the window is periodic or symmetric
options.explanation: Correct. The finite arrays and their sums differ, affecting calibration.

options.text: Coherent-gain correction alone makes every off-bin peak exact
options.explanation: It does not remove scalloping loss, neighbouring-tone interference or other finite-record effects.

options.text: Lower side lobes come with a wider main lobe than a rectangular window
options.explanation: Correct. Distant leakage suppression trades against discrimination of close tones.

options.text: The same weight sum alone is sufficient for noise PSD normalisation
options.explanation: PSD scaling instead depends on squared window weights and sample rate.

questions.workedExample:
1. State the actual finite Hann convention.
2. Check the main-lobe versus side-lobe trade-off for the measurement.
3. Use the weight sum to correct an appropriate coherent tone.
4. Treat off-bin amplitude and noise density as separate estimation problems with their own normalisations.

lessons.title: More bins do not mean more observation
lessons.summary: Use zero padding to sample a spectrum more finely without mistaking it for new resolving power.
lessons.body:
**Zero padding** appends zeros to an acquired record before its FFT. The longer transform evaluates the same finite-record spectrum at more closely spaced frequencies. A plotted peak looks smoother and a grid-based peak search can land closer to its true location. No new measurements have been made.

The important distinction is between the spacing of the displayed frequency grid and the ability to distinguish neighbouring tones. Both are sometimes called **frequency resolution**, so say which you mean.

## Keep observation and transform length separate

The acquired sample count and sample rate determine how long you observed the signal. The FFT length includes any appended zeros and determines the grid spacing. Padding changes the second length while leaving the first unchanged.

For example, acquire 64 samples at 640 samples per second: a tenth-second record. Its unpadded bins are 10 Hz apart. Pad it to 256 points and the grid becomes 2.5 Hz apart, but the acquired observation remains a tenth of a second.

```formula reference
T = N / F_s
Δf = F_s / M
where
T: acquired record duration, in seconds, using N sample intervals
N: acquired sample count
F_s: sample rate, in samples per second, expressed in hertz
M: FFT length, including appended zeros, at least N
Δf: displayed frequency-grid spacing, in hertz
In words: acquired duration comes from the real sample count and sample rate; displayed bin spacing comes from the sample rate and the FFT length, including padding.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: enlarging a photograph
> Enlarging an existing photograph can make its shapes easier to inspect. It does not capture details that the camera never recorded.
>
> **How it maps:** Extra FFT points sample the existing finite-record spectrum more densely; extra acquired samples can supply new observation information.
>
> **Where it stops:** Zero padding is exact evaluation on a denser frequency grid, not a camera's pixel interpolation algorithm. Its usefulness and limitations follow from the record's transform.

## Choose the change that solves the problem

If a peak falls between coarse grid points, padding can improve the display and the search grid. For a 73 Hz cosine in the example above, the largest unpadded bin is labelled 70 Hz and the padded one 72.5 Hz. The closer label does not establish exact frequency or measurement uncertainty: leakage, noise, the finite record and other tones can bias the estimate.

If two tones blend into one broad feature, padding alone cannot narrow the window's main lobe in hertz. Collect a longer record if the tones stay steady long enough. That can narrow the spectral features, but window shape, relative tone levels and noise still govern whether the tones can be separated. A longer observation can also mix changes that happen during it.

## Preserve amplitude calibration

Appending zeros should not make the same tone physically smaller. For coherent-tone calibration, retain the original acquired sample count when there was no taper, or the original window-weight sum when there was a taper. Dividing by the longer padded length would falsely reduce amplitude. Keep that calibration issue separate from off-bin peak error.

## Key takeaways

- Padding gives a denser grid without a longer observation.
- More acquired time can narrow spectral features when the signal remains steady; padding cannot.
- A peak's grid label is an estimate, and padding must not change coherent-tone amplitude scaling.

## Further reading

- [NumPy: FFT length and zero padding](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)
- [Steven W. Smith: Fourier transform properties](https://www.dspguide.com/CH10.PDF)

questions.prompt: You append zeros to an acquired record and compute a longer FFT. Which change should you expect?

options.text: A longer physical observation of the signal
options.explanation: Zeros appended by software are not new acquired measurements.

options.text: More closely spaced frequency-grid points over the same finite-record spectrum
options.explanation: Correct. Padding evaluates the existing record at more frequencies without changing its observation duration.

options.text: Guaranteed separation of two previously blended tones
options.explanation: The window's physical main-lobe width has not narrowed, and no new signal information was acquired.

questions.workedExample:
1. Keep the acquired samples, sample rate and window fixed.
2. Appending zeros changes only the transform length.
3. The evaluated frequency points move closer together, making the plot and peak search finer.
4. The original observation duration and ability to separate nearby tones have not improved merely from that padding.

questions.prompt: A padded spectrum has a peak at 72.5 Hz on a 2.5 Hz grid. Which report is justified by that fact alone?

options.text: The true frequency is exactly 72.5 Hz
options.explanation: A grid maximum can be biased by leakage, finite observation, noise and other tones.

options.text: The measurement uncertainty is exactly 2.5 Hz
options.explanation: Grid spacing alone does not determine a measurement uncertainty interval.

options.text: The largest evaluated spectral magnitude occurs at the 72.5 Hz grid point
options.explanation: Correct. This describes the actual discrete search result without claiming unverified accuracy.

questions.workedExample:
1. Zero padding evaluates more frequencies of the same finite record.
2. A maximum selects one of those evaluated frequencies.
3. It is a grid-based estimate, rather than proof of the exact generating frequency.
4. Accuracy needs an estimator model, observation assumptions and noise/interference analysis.

questions.prompt: A steady pair of close tones is difficult to distinguish. Which statements are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Acquire a longer record if the tones remain steady
options.explanation: Correct. A longer observation can narrow the window's spectral features in physical frequency.

options.text: Zero padding alone narrows the existing window's main lobe in hertz
options.explanation: It only samples the existing spectral shape on a denser grid.

options.text: Consider window shape, relative tone levels and noise
options.explanation: Correct. All affect practical tone discrimination.

options.text: Divide a padded coherent-tone FFT by padded length regardless of original window
options.explanation: That falsely changes amplitude when only zeros are appended; use the original sample count or weight sum as appropriate.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask whether the missing distinction is caused by the observation/window rather than a coarse plot.
2. Extra acquired time can supply narrower spectral features if stationarity is a reasonable assumption.
3. The window and signal-to-interference conditions still matter.
4. Padding supplies a denser display and search grid, without changing the original window sum used for coherent-amplitude scaling.

lessons.title: Following frequencies through time
lessons.summary: Build a short-time spectrum and distinguish frame duration, hop spacing and frequency-grid spacing.
lessons.body:
A single FFT describes everything in its record together. If a machine first vibrates at one frequency and later another, that spectrum does not show their order. A **short-time Fourier transform**, or **STFT**, instead analyses successive short, windowed records called **analysis frames**.

A **spectrogram** displays a squared-magnitude or power-related version of those transforms: time on one axis, frequency on another and strength shown by colour. Check what the colours mean. A coloured plot is not automatically a calibrated PSD.

## Frame length controls what gets blended

Each frame observes a span of time. A longer frame gives narrower spectral features for steady tones, making close frequencies easier to distinguish under suitable conditions. It also combines events across a longer interval. If a tone changes inside the frame, both its earlier and later frequencies can contribute to that frame.

A shorter frame localises changes more closely in time, but broadens its frequency features. Choose the frame length for the event you want to understand rather than assuming a more detailed-looking plot has resolved everything.

## Hop controls how often you look

The **hop** is the distance in samples between neighbouring frame starts. A hop shorter than the frame length makes the frames overlap. Reducing the hop gives more frequent spectra by sharing more samples. It does not shorten each frame's observation or remove its time-frequency trade-off.

For example, a frame can observe 125 milliseconds while another frame starts every 31.25 milliseconds. The frequent updates still each mix information over a 125-millisecond span.

```formula reference
T_w = L / F_s
T_h = H / F_s
where
T_w: duration observed by each frame, in seconds
T_h: interval between consecutive frame starts, in seconds
L: number of acquired samples per frame
H: hop length, in samples
F_s: sample rate, in samples per second
In words: frame duration is the frame's sample count divided by the sample rate; update spacing uses the hop count instead, so more overlap gives more updates without shortening the observation.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: overlapping snapshots
> Take long-exposure photographs at frequent intervals. Starting another exposure sooner creates more photographs, but each photograph still blends movement over its own exposure.
>
> **How it maps:** Frame length is the observation span and hop is the interval between observations. Overlapping frames share samples.
>
> **Where it stops:** The STFT measures oscillation components using a window, rather than brightness. A smaller hop cannot improve the window's intrinsic frequency discrimination.

## Read a spectrogram's contract

Before comparing two plots, establish the window and frame length, hop, FFT length, time labels and boundary policy. Extra zero padding gives more frequency-grid positions inside each frame; it does not lengthen the acquired frame.

Some implementations label frames by their centres, others by their starts. Some extend the signal at the edges, while others omit incomplete frames. A centred window near an edge can include assumed samples outside the actual record. These choices affect apparent event timing and edge content.

Finally match the strength normalisation and colour units. Amplitude, squared magnitude and PSD use different normalisations. SciPy's `ShortTimeFFT` exposes frame, hop and scaling choices; record the settings with the plot so another reader can interpret it.

## Key takeaways

- An STFT follows changing spectra using successive windowed frames.
- Frame length controls the observation span; hop controls update spacing.
- Match time labels, boundaries and scaling before comparing spectrograms.

## Further reading

- [SciPy: short-time Fourier transform](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.stft.html)
- [SciPy: ShortTimeFFT](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT.html)

questions.prompt: An STFT blends an abrupt tone change across a long frame. You shorten the frame at the same sample rate, keeping the same window family. What trade-off should you expect?

options.text: Less time blending, but broader frequency features for steady tones
options.explanation: Correct. A shorter frame observes a shorter interval, while its wider spectral features can make close tones harder to distinguish.

options.text: Less time blending and guaranteed separation of closer frequencies
options.explanation: Shortening the observation broadens spectral features; it does not guarantee better discrimination of close tones.

options.text: The same observation span, because only the hop controls it

lessons.title: Reduce sample rate without folding signals
lessons.summary: Set a new Nyquist limit, low-pass first and understand why keeping every second sample is insufficient.
lessons.body:
Keeping every second or third sample lowers the sample rate. It also lowers the range of frequencies that can be represented without ambiguity. A tone that was safe at the original rate can exceed the new Nyquist limit and appear as a different, lower-frequency tone.

**Decimation** combines low-pass filtering with retaining samples at a lower rate. The order matters: suppress the unwanted high frequencies before discarding samples.

## Design for the output rate

Reducing a 1200-sample-per-second signal by a factor of three gives 400 samples per second. Its new Nyquist boundary is 200 Hz, even though the original boundary was 600 Hz. Design the prefilter for the reduced rate.

```formula reference
F_o = F_i / D
f_N = F_o / 2
where
F_o: output sample rate, in samples per second, expressed in hertz
F_i: input sample rate, in samples per second, expressed in hertz
D: positive integer reduction factor
f_N: output Nyquist boundary, in hertz
In words: divide the input sample rate by the reduction factor, then halve the output rate to find its Nyquist boundary.
```

Wanted baseband content must lie strictly below that boundary. A practical low-pass also needs a transition band in which its response falls from passing wanted content to rejecting unwanted content. Do not put the wanted passband edge exactly at Nyquist and expect an instantaneous cut-off. Choose enough stopband attenuation for the alias level the application can tolerate.

## Why filtering afterwards is too late

A 350 Hz cosine is below the original Nyquist boundary in this example. Keep every third sample without filtering, and it appears as a 50 Hz cosine at the output. Discarding samples has folded the unwanted tone into the useful band; it has not erased it.

Now an actual 50 Hz input and the aliased 350 Hz input can be indistinguishable from the output samples alone. A later low-pass cannot selectively remove the alias while preserving every genuine 50 Hz component. Filter before the ambiguity occurs.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: checking before a narrow doorway
> Remove oversized items before sending a mixed delivery through a narrow doorway. Sorting afterwards cannot recover information lost when items were forced together.
>
> **How it maps:** The new rate has a smaller unambiguous frequency range. The prefilter suppresses components outside it before samples are discarded.
>
> **Where it stops:** Aliasing is an exact ambiguity between sampled oscillations, not physical damage or a queue. A real filter only attenuates unwanted components by a finite amount.

## Specify the whole rate-change operation

SciPy's `decimate` filters before reducing. `resample_poly` also combines FIR filtering and rate conversion efficiently. An API is useful, but its default filter is not evidence that your required passband and stopband specification has been met. Test across the unwanted band and inspect finite-record edges.

Record the timing convention too. A causal streaming filter has delay and startup behaviour; an offline centred or zero-phase operation has different alignment and boundary assumptions. Neither should silently substitute for the other when event times matter.

This digital prefilter protects a later digital rate reduction. It cannot repair aliasing that already happened at the original analogue-to-digital conversion, which needs its own anti-alias protection.

## Key takeaways

- The output rate sets the relevant Nyquist boundary.
- Filter before reducing, leaving a transition band and enough unwanted-band rejection.
- Record timing and edge assumptions, and keep original ADC aliasing separate from later decimation.

## Further reading

- [SciPy: decimation includes an anti-alias filter](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.decimate.html)
- [SciPy: polyphase resampling and boundary assumptions](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.resample_poly.html)

lessons.title: Increase sample rate with interpolation
lessons.summary: Follow zero insertion, spectral images and the low-pass gain needed to reconstruct between samples.
lessons.body:
**Interpolation** estimates samples at new time positions from an existing record. Increasing the output sample rate gives more values to pass to another system, but they are computed estimates, not extra physical measurements. It cannot recover frequency distinctions already lost to aliasing.

Integer-rate interpolation has two conceptual steps: insert zero placeholders between the original samples, then apply a reconstruction low-pass filter. Efficient implementations can combine these steps without explicitly calculating every zero.

## New positions preserve the original times

To double the rate, put each original sample in every other output position. Interpret the result at twice the original sample rate. Original values then retain their original time positions; the extra positions fall between them.

For a constant sequence of ones, the intermediate sequence alternates ones and zeros. Those zeros do not claim the physical signal stopped between observations. They reserve positions for the filtering step.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: filling a timetable
> Put the known appointments into a timetable with twice as many time slots. Empty slots reserve positions; they do not mean the activity stopped.
>
> **How it maps:** Original samples retain their timing while zero placeholders create new positions. The filter estimates values at and around those positions.
>
> **Where it stops:** Signal interpolation depends on a bandwidth assumption and a numerical filter, not judgement about appointments. It cannot invent unknown high-frequency information.

## Filter images and restore the scale

Zero insertion produces **spectral images**: copies of the original baseband spectrum within the enlarged frequency range. A reconstruction low-pass retains the wanted band and suppresses those images. They are still separated from the wanted baseband, so filtering can remove them before any later reduction folds them together.

The filter must also have appropriate gain. With one zero after every original sample, the constant sequence's average is halved. A unity-DC-gain low-pass would keep that reduced average. If no other scale correction is present, a factor-two interpolator needs a filter with DC gain two. More generally, the required DC gain equals the zero-insertion factor, with corresponding passband gain where faithful reconstruction is wanted.

A three-coefficient filter with weights `[0.5, 1.0, 0.5]` illustrates this for doubling. Their sum is two. It fills the interior constant sequence back to one and provides linear interpolation between successive original values after accounting for delay. Its image suppression is too gradual for demanding applications; it is a useful model rather than a production specification.

## Compare implementations fairly

That toy filter used causally has one high-rate-sample delay and edge transients. An offline centred API can produce different timing and edge values while still performing its documented operation. Match the filter, scaling, output-length and boundary conventions before comparing arrays.

**Resampling** can increase by one integer factor and decrease by another. SciPy's `resample_poly` combines zero insertion, FIR filtering and reduction using **polyphase** computation. It supplies the required internal amplitude scaling, so do not multiply its default output by the insertion factor again.

Its default boundary model assumes zeros beyond the finite input. A filter for the intermediate increased rate must both suppress interpolation images and protect the final reduced rate from aliasing. Inspect timing and boundary behaviour as well as the interior frequency response.

## Key takeaways

- Zero placeholders reserve time positions; low-pass filtering forms the interpolated signal.
- Reconstruction needs the right gain as well as image suppression.
- More output values cannot undo original aliasing or replace new measurements.

## Further reading

- [SciPy: upsample, FIR filter and downsample](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.upfirdn.html)
- [SciPy: polyphase resampling](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.resample_poly.html)

lessons.title: FFT convolution without wrapping the tail
lessons.summary: Turn circular FFT multiplication into full linear convolution and preserve block tails with overlap-add.
lessons.body:
FFT multiplication can calculate convolution efficiently, but the transform's boundary model matters. A fixed-length DFT treats its input as repeating. Multiplying the transforms and taking an inverse FFT therefore gives **circular convolution**: contributions beyond the chosen length wrap back to the beginning.

Ordinary finite filtering with zero extension needs linear convolution instead. The solution is to reserve space for the complete output, including its filter tail, before transforming.

## Make room before multiplying

For a four-sample input and a three-coefficient FIR, the full output occupies six positions. Pad both transforms to at least that full length. Using only the length of the longer input generally leaves too little room.

```formula essential
Q = N + K − 1
M ≥ Q
where
Q: full linear-convolution output length, in samples
N: input record length, in samples
K: FIR coefficient count
M: shared FFT length used for both inputs
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: the full output needs the input length plus the filter length minus one positions; both FFTs must be at least that long to avoid wrapping the tail into the beginning.
```

A longer FFT can be chosen for efficiency. After the inverse transform, keep the full linear output length; extra padded positions are not additional physical output. Small floating-point errors can remain.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a circular calendar
> Write a long task schedule on a repeating weekly calendar. Anything that spills past Sunday appears back under Monday unless you reserve enough distinct dates.
>
> **How it maps:** Circular convolution wraps the tail into earlier positions. Sufficient padding reserves space for every linear-convolution contribution before the repetition begins.
>
> **Where it stops:** The FFT combines numeric contributions by addition, and its wrap is an exact mathematical boundary rule. Padding removes that wrap for finite linear convolution; it does not remove a filter's actual tail.

## Recognise wraparound in a result

For input `[1, 2, 3, 4]` and FIR `[1, 1, 1]`, full linear convolution is `[1, 3, 6, 9, 7, 4]`. A four-point FFT product instead returns `[8, 7, 6, 9]`. The final tail has been added into the beginning, not discarded or substituted for the first samples.

This gives a useful diagnosis: if the end of a filtered record contaminates its beginning, inspect transform length and padding before changing the filter coefficients. Compare with direct full convolution on a small input to check the boundary behaviour.

## Add block responses at their original positions

For a long signal, **overlap-add** processes input blocks separately with the same FIR. Each block needs sufficient FFT padding for its own full convolution. Place that result at the output position corresponding to the block's original start.

Adjacent results overlap because each block keeps producing a filter tail after its last input sample. Add contributions at shared positions. Concatenating full block outputs shifts later responses; overwriting the overlap loses contributions.

When full finite output is requested, retain the last tail after the final input block. A streaming implementation also needs buffering, latency and flushing policies. Overlap-add does not guarantee zero latency. SciPy provides `fftconvolve` for FFT convolution and `oaconvolve` for overlap-add; actual speed depends on lengths and hardware.

## Key takeaways

- FFT multiplication naturally uses circular boundaries.
- Pad both transforms for the full linear output to prevent wraparound.
- Overlap-add combines shared positions and keeps the final tail when full output is required.

## Further reading

- [Steven W. Smith: FFT convolution and overlap-add](https://www.dspguide.com/CH18.PDF)
- [SciPy: full FFT convolution](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.fftconvolve.html)
- [SciPy: overlap-add convolution](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.oaconvolve.html)

lessons.title: A reproducible vibration measurement
lessons.summary: Combine known timing, RMS, causal filtering and a calibrated spectrum with explicit synthetic checks.
lessons.body:
Before trusting a measurement chain, test it on a synthetic signal with known truth. A real vibration sensor adds calibration uncertainty, noise, drift and timing error. A generated record lets you first ask whether the processing behaves as intended.

This experiment uses an acceleration offset, a wanted 64 Hz tone and a 192 Hz interferer. The task is to preserve the wanted tone, reduce the interferer and explain the measured output. It tests numerical processing on a host computer; it does not establish physical sensor accuracy or device timing performance.

## State a reproducible contract

Use the following fixed setup, with no random noise or external files. Acceleration values are in metres per second squared.

| Setting | Choice |
|---|---|
| Sample rate | 1024 samples per second |
| Acquired length | 1280 samples |
| Constant offset | 0.4 |
| Wanted cosine peak | 2 at 64 Hz |
| Interfering cosine peak | 0.6 at 192 Hz |

Start both cosines at their positive peak at sample zero. They complete whole cycles over this acquired record, so their mean is zero and the measured mean should be the stated offset, allowing numerical rounding.

Remove that measured mean before analysing AC RMS, so the constant offset does not count as vibration around the mean. Both oscillating tones remain. RMS describes average squared size followed by a square root; it is not the sum or average of the tone peaks. For these whole-cycle, orthogonal cosines, mean-square contributions add because their cross-products average to zero.

## Separate filter behaviour from measurement behaviour

Apply a causal three-tap moving average with equal weights and zero initial state. Each output averages the current input and two preceding inputs. SciPy's `lfilter` can implement this causal operation; an offline zero-phase filter would be a different contract.

Discard the first 256 outputs, then analyse the remaining 1024. This keeps filter startup outside the analysed segment. Both tones complete whole cycles there too. The symmetric three-tap filter has one input-sample delay: discarding startup does not remove that delay when interpreting time events.

Apply a periodic Hann to the analysed segment. Use its actual weight sum for coherent-tone amplitude calibration, doubling only paired interior bins. Both test tones are interior bins, well away from DC and Nyquist. Use a separate frequency-response calculation to predict each output tone before comparing with the measured spectrum.

## Interpret the checks

The wanted output peak is approximately 1.899 and the interferer's approximately 0.353, in the same acceleration units as the input. The interferer is reduced, not eliminated. The wanted tone is also attenuated, so its output peak must not be reported as the original input peak.

Make separate checks for mean removal, RMS, filter response and spectrum scaling. A coherent-amplitude assertion can reveal a scaling or filtering error, but it cannot by itself prove time alignment, physical calibration or real-time performance. Inspect time events as well if timing matters.

A longer, suitably designed filter may reject the interferer better, with different delay and transition behaviour. On a real record, document sample-clock accuracy, calibration, detrending, window, bandwidth and transient handling. A peak's bin label alone does not supply an uncertainty interval.

## Key takeaways

- Known synthetic input lets you check each processing stage against a stated contract.
- Predict the filter's effect before interpreting an output peak as an input measurement.
- Numerical agreement establishes the tested behaviour; physical calibration and timing need their own evidence.

## Further reading

- [SciPy: causal filtering and initial conditions](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.lfilter.html)
- [SciPy: frequency response of a digital filter](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.freqz.html)
- [SciPy: periodic and symmetric Hann windows](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.windows.hann.html)
- [NumPy: FFT conventions](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.fft.html)
